name: Seoul Gimpo International Airport
before:
Seoul's second airport, at the far western edge of the city about 15 km from the centre, and much closer in than Incheon. It was the country's main international airport until Incheon replaced it in 2001, and carried over 23 million passengers in 2015.

What makes it valuable now is a small set of short international routes into other cities' close-in airports. Gimpo flies to Haneda in Tokyo, Hongqiao in Shanghai, Kansai in Osaka, Beijing Capital and Songshan in Taipei. For a client on business in any of those cities, that pairing saves a long transfer at both ends.

One booking note. Gimpo used to hold the code SEL, which now stands for all Seoul airports in reservation systems, so check which airport a fare actually uses.

The airfield was built in 1939 as a Japanese army base, with runways laid on rock hauled by hand by Korean labourers, and played a major part in the Korean War as Kimpo Air Base, the name the United States Air Force gave it.
after:
Seoul's city airport, at the western edge of town about 15 km from the centre, and much closer in than Incheon. It was Seoul's main international airport until Incheon opened in 2001.

Its international flights include Songshan, Taipei's own city airport. For a client on business in Taipei, flying between the two saves a long transfer at both ends.

The airfield dates from 1939, when the Japanese army built it. A presidential decree made it Gimpo International Airport in 1958.

claims.note: Replaces 'Gimpo flies to Haneda in Tokyo, Hongqiao in Shanghai, Kansai in Osaka, Beijing Capital and Songshan in Taipei'. Only Songshan has a second current source that could be read: Taiwan's official schedule data (MOTC's TDX, saved for Songshan on 23 September 2026 and copied here) lists flights from Songshan (TSA) to Gimpo (GMP) in late September 2026, and the Taipei Metro calls Songshan an airport right in the city core. The operator's own schedule and live flight pages build their tables by script, so the saved copies carry no routes; the other four routes rest on Wikipedia alone (cut below). 'Include' because Wikipedia lists others.
